node.title: A deceptive division at Mecone
node.text: Prometheus prepares two portions of an ox: useful meat disguised beneath an unattractive covering, and bones made inviting with fat. Hesiod…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Prometheus prepares two portions of an ox: useful meat disguised beneath an unattractive covering, and bones made inviting with fat. Hesiod presents Zeus as recognizing the trick, yet taking the portion that explains why mortals burn bones for the gods. The episode describes a fraught separation of divine and human shares rather than a simple contest won without consequences.

node.title: Fire, punishment, and a burden above the earth
node.text: After Zeus withholds fire, Prometheus steals it in a fennel stalk. Zeus's retaliation includes Prometheus's binding and an eagle that…

node.title: The telling
node.text: After Zeus withholds fire, Prometheus steals it in a fennel stalk. Zeus's retaliation includes Prometheus's binding and an eagle that consumes his regenerating liver; Heracles eventually kills the eagle with Zeus's assent. Atlas, another brother, supports the broad heaven at the world's limits. The familiar image of Atlas carrying Earth should not replace Hesiod's description of his burden.

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hesiod insists that Zeus does not strip Hecate of her earlier honors. She can assist speakers, warriors, athletes, riders, fishers, and herders, granting or withholding success. This expansive portrait matters because reducing her to a single later association with witchcraft would hide much of what the Theogony actually praises.

node.title: A torch beside Demeter
node.text: Hecate hears Persephone's cry but does not see the abductor. She tells Demeter exactly that limited knowledge, then accompanies her to…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hecate hears Persephone's cry but does not see the abductor. She tells Demeter exactly that limited knowledge, then accompanies her to Helios, who can identify what happened. After mother and daughter reunite, Hecate embraces Persephone and becomes her companion. The hymn gives her a sustained role without making her the architect of the abduction or the final settlement.

node.title: Metis and the succession that must not happen
node.text: After the overthrow of Cronus, the danger of another divine succession remains. Metis is destined to bear Athena and then a son who could…

node.title: The telling
node.text: After the overthrow of Cronus, the danger of another divine succession remains. Metis is destined to bear Athena and then a son who could become ruler. Zeus swallows the pregnant Metis, following the warning of Gaia and Ouranos. Athena later emerges from his head. The family tree therefore preserves Metis as mother, even though the visible birth takes place through Zeus.

node.title: A settlement that another god contests
node.text: In Iliad 15, Poseidon recalls the drawing of lots that assigned him the sea, Hades the underworld, and Zeus the sky, while Earth and…

node.title: The telling
node.text: In Iliad 15, Poseidon recalls the drawing of lots that assigned him the sea, Hades the underworld, and Zeus the sky, while Earth and Olympus remained shared. He protests Zeus's attempt to command him as a subordinate. The disagreement shows that supremacy and inherited shares can coexist uneasily; Zeus's government contains negotiation and resentment as well as obedience.

node.title: The telling
node.text: In the Apollo hymn, Leto struggles in childbirth on Delos while other goddesses attend. Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, remains unaware on Olympus because Hera keeps her away. Iris is sent to bring her, and Apollo is finally born. Hera's role makes a birth into a dispute over divine status rather than a purely private family event.

node.title: Hephaestus and incompatible family memories
node.text: Hesiod says Hera bears Hephaestus without a male partner in anger toward Zeus. The Library preserves that account but also acknowledges a…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hesiod says Hera bears Hephaestus without a male partner in anger toward Zeus. The Library preserves that account but also acknowledges a version naming Zeus as father. In Iliad 18, Hephaestus recalls Hera rejecting him and Thetis and Eurynome sheltering him. These passages should be read in their own settings rather than combined into a seamless biography with every detail fixed.

node.title: The telling
node.text: In the Library's account of the contest for Attica, Poseidon strikes the Acropolis and produces a salt-water source; Athena plants an olive. Twelve gods judge the dispute, with Cecrops as witness. Athena receives the land, and Poseidon responds with a flood. This version should not be silently replaced by accounts involving a popular vote or a different first gift.

node.text: Hesiod connects Athena's birth to Zeus's swallowing of Metis. The short Athena hymn concentrates instead on the spectacle: the goddess…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hesiod connects Athena's birth to Zeus's swallowing of Metis. The short Athena hymn concentrates instead on the spectacle: the goddess springs from Zeus's head in armor, and the surrounding world trembles before her appearance. These emphases can be compared without treating the hymn's silence about Metis as proof that Athena has no mother.

node.title: An olive and the work of human hands

node.title: The telling
node.text: Athena's olive secures Attica in the Library's contest narrative. Another short hymn praises Athena together with Hephaestus for teaching useful arts, imagining human dwellings transformed by skilled work. Read together, these texts connect her civic presence to cultivated land, protection, and practical knowledge, rather than reducing her to a goddess of battle alone.

When they worry about supporting themselves, he points them toward the offerings they will receive. The hymn links divine conquest with the practical creation of a sanctuary community.

node.title: Actaeon: a story with an explicit alternative
node.text: The Library reports the familiar account in which Actaeon sees Artemis bathing, is changed into a deer, and is killed by his own hounds.…

node.title: The telling
node.text: The Library reports the familiar account in which Actaeon sees Artemis bathing, is changed into a deer, and is killed by his own hounds. But it also records Acusilaus's explanation that Zeus was angry because Actaeon sought Semele. The outcome is shared while its cause differs; the collection labels this disagreement instead of presenting one motive as universal.

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hermes finds a tortoise and transforms its shell into a lyre. Soon he steals fifty cattle belonging to Apollo, reversing their tracks and disguising his own footsteps with improvised sandals. The hymn places musical creativity and deception side by side: the same quick intelligence produces something beautiful and creates the problem that brings Apollo to his mother's cave.

node.title: From accusation to exchange

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hermes denies the theft with elaborate appeals to his infant helplessness. Zeus laughs and orders a resolution. When Apollo hears the lyre, hostility gives way to admiration, and the brothers negotiate gifts and responsibilities. Hermes's new standing arises through persuasion and exchange. In the Demeter hymn, that recognized mediator can travel to Hades and escort Persephone back to her mother.

Its imagery extends beyond the battlefield for which the armor is intended. One useful reading is that the shield holds the wider human world endangered by war; that is an interpretation of the described scenes, not a separate ancient plot event.

The narrator repeatedly marks Persephone's unwillingness, so a faithful retelling should not replace the seizure with a voluntary romantic departure.

node.title: A return with a continuing cost
node.text: Hades allows Persephone to leave with Hermes but gives her pomegranate seed so she cannot remain permanently above. In her own account, he…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hades allows Persephone to leave with Hermes but gives her pomegranate seed so she cannot remain permanently above. In her own account, he forces her to taste it. The settlement assigns one-third of the year below and two-thirds with her mother and the gods. Her joyful reunion is therefore real but incomplete; the hymn does not specify the familiar modern six-seed arrangement.

node.title: The ruler below and the imposed marriage
node.text: The Demeter hymn presents Hades both as Persephone's abductor and as a king who promises her extensive honors. His offer of rank does not…

node.title: The telling
node.text: The Demeter hymn presents Hades both as Persephone's abductor and as a king who promises her extensive honors. His offer of rank does not undo the coercion that brought her there. When Zeus orders her release, Hades complies but uses the pomegranate to secure her return. Family hierarchy, sovereignty, and control over movement intersect in his response.

node.title: Orpheus receives a conditional exception
node.text: In the Library's concise account, Orpheus descends to recover Eurydice after a snake kills her. He persuades Pluto, a name for the ruler…

node.title: The telling
node.text: In the Library's concise account, Orpheus descends to recover Eurydice after a snake kills her. He persuades Pluto, a name for the ruler below, to send her back if he does not turn to look before reaching his home. Orpheus turns and loses her again. The exception depends on a condition; the story does not abolish the boundary between living and dead.

node.text: Hestia's importance appears through constancy, hospitality, and repeated ritual attention. Her shorter stories can be easy to overlook beside…

node.text: No biological children in the principal traditions used here. Athena’s care of Erichthonius is distinct from biological maternity.

node.title: A choice to remain unmarried
node.text: The Aphrodite hymn names Hestia among the goddesses beyond Aphrodite's power. Apollo and Poseidon seek her, but she refuses marriage and…

node.title: The telling
node.text: The Aphrodite hymn names Hestia among the goddesses beyond Aphrodite's power. Apollo and Poseidon seek her, but she refuses marriage and swears a lasting oath of virginity with her hand on Zeus's head. Zeus grants her an honored place in the house. The passage presents her status as a deliberate choice, not as an absence of significance.

node.title: The first and last libation
node.text: Hymn 29 associates Hestia with an enduring place in divine and human dwellings and with offerings at the opening and close of a feast. It…

node.title: The telling
node.text: Hymn 29 associates Hestia with an enduring place in divine and human dwellings and with offerings at the opening and close of a feast. It also invokes Hermes alongside her, bringing a mobile mediator into the same prayer as the hearth's stable presence. The pairing is ritual cooperation, not evidence that the two gods form a married couple.

node.title: Identification is a historical relationship, not a rule that two cults or narratives were interchangeable.
Zeus or Jupiter
node.text:
Roman; 1st–3rd century CE. Met 96.18.6.
A Roman statuette catalogued as Zeus or Jupiter makes the shared visual vocabulary and uncertain naming visible.

node.title: Read across each pair; the contrast matters as much as the shared iconography.
Comparisons 1–3
node.text: Zeus / Jupiter · Hera / Juno · Poseidon / Neptune

node.title: Zeus
node.text: Both names identify a ruling sky god in the familiar literary correspondence. Virgil places Jupiter at the center of a specifically Roman promise: he reassures Venus that Aeneas’ descendants will lead toward Rome and an extended future of rule.

node.title: Jupiter
node.text:
The Roman future is part of the Aeneid’s political imagination, not an episode silently added to Homer.

A shared thunderbolt does not establish identical local cults.

node.title: Hera
node.text: Ovid makes Juno argue that June belongs to her, invoking her standing as Jupiter’s wife and her authority over marriages. The familiar association with Hera is present, but the calendar gives the goddess a Roman civic setting.

node.title: Juno
node.text:
Ovid stages rival explanations of the month’s name rather than one neutral etymology.

Marriage and royal status are points of comparison, not a complete biography.

node.title: Poseidon
node.text: Virgil’s Neptune restores a sea disturbed by winds released through Juno’s intervention. The trident and maritime authority recall Poseidon, while the comparison of the calming god to a respected statesman gives the scene a civic vocabulary.

node.title: Neptune
node.text:
The Aeneid’s calming action contrasts with Poseidon’s hostility to Odysseus.

Read what the god does in a particular poem before treating a name match as an explanation.

Comparisons 4–6
node.text: Athena / Minerva · Apollo / Apollo · Artemis / Diana

node.title: Athena
node.text: At the Quinquatrus, Ovid calls on students and practitioners of many skills to honor Minerva. Weaving, teaching, medicine and artistic work join martial imagery. This gives the Athena–Minerva comparison a concrete calendar and occupational setting.

node.title: Minerva
node.text:
Minerva is not adequately described as simply a goddess of war.

Ovid also offers competing explanations of the title Minerva Capta.

node.title: Apollo
node.text: Apollo retains his familiar name in Roman literature. Horace’s public hymn invokes his healing and prophetic powers, then connects the god’s Palatine altars with hopes for Rome and Latium. Continuity of name coexists with a distinct setting.

node.title: Apollo
node.text:
A Roman appropriation need not involve renaming.

The hymn expresses civic wishes; it does not prove that all Romans understood Apollo identically.

node.title: Artemis
node.text: Catullus addresses Diana through multiple titles associated with childbirth, crossroads and the moon, while naming her as Latona’s daughter. Horace places Diana alongside Apollo in a Roman choral appeal. These poems show overlapping functions within a particular reception.

node.title: Diana
node.text:
The lunar title does not erase distinctions between Artemis and Selene in earlier Greek genealogies.

Diana’s Roman sanctuaries and public prayers deserve their own context.

Comparisons 7–9
node.text: Aphrodite / Venus · Ares / Mars · Hermes / Mercury

node.title: Aphrodite
node.text: Venus is associated with Aphrodite’s erotic power, but Roman poetry also makes her Aeneas’ mother and an ancestral figure for a Roman future. Ovid’s April discussion joins attraction, fertility and genealogy to the organization of the year.

node.title: Venus
node.text:
Ancestral claims add political work to the familiar imagery of love.

Do not make Roman descent claims into historical biological evidence.

node.title: Ares
node.text: The Ares–Mars correspondence is useful but incomplete. Cato’s agricultural prayer asks Mars to protect fields, crops, flocks and the household from disease and destruction. Ovid’s March opening also makes Mars the father of Rome’s founding twins.

node.title: Mars
node.text:
Agricultural protection does not mean that Mars lacks a military role.

A ritual prescription and a poetic foundation story offer different kinds of evidence.

node.title: Hermes
node.text: Ovid’s Mercury combines swift mediation, eloquence and association with trade. His account of merchants sprinkling themselves and their goods turns comic when the prayer asks forgiveness for past deception and room for profitable future lies.

node.title: Mercury
node.text:
The dishonest prayer is Ovid’s satirical presentation, not an instruction to assume every merchant’s conduct.

Commercial ritual gives the correspondence with Hermes a Roman social setting.

Comparisons 10–12
node.text: Demeter / Ceres · Dionysus / Liber / Bacchus · Hestia / Vesta

node.title: Demeter
node.text: Ovid retells the search for the abducted daughter within the April observances of Ceres. The story associates a divine mother’s loss with disruption of nourishment, but its ritual framing and details belong to this Roman poetic treatment.

node.title: Ceres
node.text:
The Roman telling should be compared with, not substituted for, the Homeric Hymn to Demeter.

Shared grain imagery does not exhaust the institutions surrounding either goddess.

node.title: Dionysus
node.text: In Ovid’s Liberalia passage, Bacchic stories help explain honey cakes and the presence of older women selling offerings. The poem also explores why boys take the adult toga on Liber’s day, linking divine names with social transition.

node.title: Liber / Bacchus
node.text:
Liber, Bacchus and Dionysus overlap in reception; their histories should not be reduced to a single dictionary substitution.

Ovid proposes several explanations rather than certifying one origin.

node.title: Hestia
node.text: Vesta’s fire and virginity recall Hestia, yet Ovid describes a specifically Roman sacred building, attendants, and civic responsibilities. He distinguishes the living fire from an imagined statue inside the shrine and connects ritual protection with the city.

node.title: Vesta
node.text:
Domestic and public hearths are related without being the same institution.

The Vestals’ office is more than a narrative trait transferred from a Greek goddess.

Comparisons 13–15
node.text: Hephaestus / Vulcan · Hades / Plouton / Dis · Persephone / Proserpina

node.title: Hephaestus
node.text: Virgil’s Vulcan answers Venus’ request by preparing armor for Aeneas. The divine smith recalls Hephaestus, but the resulting shield displays a Roman historical future, culminating in Actium, rather than the broad human world on Achilles’ shield.

node.title: Vulcan
node.text:
The shield’s images belong to the Aeneid’s interpretation of Roman destiny.

A shared craft role allows literary comparison without making the artifacts interchangeable.

node.title: Hades / Plouton
node.text: Ovid’s account of Proserpina’s abduction names the underworld ruler Dis and relates him to Jupiter. That narrative draws on the family and marriage structure familiar from Greek accounts while reshaping its setting and speakers.

node.title: Dis
node.text:
Dis, Pluto and other Latin underworld names require attention to the author and passage.

This ruler of the dead is not simply a Roman version of the Christian devil.

node.title: Persephone
node.text: Ovid tells how Proserpina’s eating below prevents an unrestricted return. Jupiter divides her time between her mother and husband. The daughter’s movement connects two domains, but the Latin poem’s settlement must be read in its own terms.

node.title: Proserpina
node.text:
Ovid’s equal division differs from the Homeric Hymn’s one-third below and two-thirds above.

Do not present one seasonal arithmetic as the rule for every ancient telling.

Comparisons 16–18
node.text: Cronus / Saturn · Rhea / Ops · Gaia / Tellus / Terra

node.title: Cronus
node.text: Ovid’s Janus recalls receiving Saturn after Jupiter expelled him from heavenly rule. A ship on old coinage becomes a reminder of that arrival, while the Italian setting gives the Greek succession pattern a new geographical and cultural role.

node.title: Saturn
node.text:
Saturn’s Italian reception is not simply the next chapter of Hesiod’s Theogony.

A poetic explanation of names and coins is evidence of interpretation, not archaeological proof of a divine migration.

Hesiod; divine genealogy and the establishment of Zeus’ rule
Theogony
node.text: Origins become an argument about power. Births, conflicts, alliances and the distribution of honors explain how a populated cosmos reaches Zeus’ kingship. The poem combines family catalogues with episodes of violence and negotiation; it is one…

node.title: The work’s argument
node.text: Origins become an argument about power. Births, conflicts, alliances and the distribution of honors explain how a populated cosmos reaches Zeus’ kingship. The poem combines family catalogues with episodes of violence and negotiation; it is one attributed account, not a universal mythological canon.

node.title: Reading sequence 1–4 · Hesiod; divine genealogy and the establishment of Zeus’ rule
Reading sequence 1–4
node.text: Who authorizes the song? · From first beings to a broken succession · Many kinds of divine power · A child escapes being swallowed

node.title: Who authorizes the song?
node.text:
1–115

The Muses give the singer authority while claiming command of convincing falsehood as well as truth. Their gifts connect poetry, memory and persuasive judgment, preparing the reader to consider how a cosmic history becomes credible.

node.title: From first beings to a broken succession
node.text:
116–210

Chaos, Earth and other initial powers precede generations of descendants. Uranus confines his children, and Gaia helps Cronus attack him. The violence produces further beings, including the account of Aphrodite’s emergence from the sea.

node.title: Many kinds of divine power
node.text:
211–452

Night, Sea and Titan families populate the world with natural forces, social experiences and monstrous figures. Hecate’s extended praise shows that divine standing involves allotted honors across domains, not merely a position on a descent chart.

node.title: A child escapes being swallowed
node.text:
453–506

Cronus swallows Rhea’s children to prevent displacement. Rhea conceals Zeus and substitutes a stone. The children return, and Zeus gains allies and weapons, reversing suppression through a combination of deception and recovered kinship.

Reading sequence 5–7
node.text: Sacrifice, fire and a costly gift · Victory and the boundaries of the world · Marriages and new generations

node.title: Sacrifice, fire and a costly gift
node.text:
507–616

The Iapetid family leads into Prometheus’ contest with Zeus over sacrifice and fire. The crafted woman answers the stolen fire in a deeply gendered explanation of human hardship. This account differs in detail from Works and Days.

node.title: Victory and the boundaries of the world
node.text:
617–885

The Hundred-Handers help defeat the Titans. A description of the cosmic depths situates confinement and divine boundaries. Zeus then defeats Typhoeus, and the gods invite him to rule and distribute their honors.

node.title: Marriages and new generations
node.text:
886–1022

Zeus’ swallowing of Metis prevents another succession threat. Divine unions organize new powers and families; the closing movement turns toward goddesses with mortal partners and heroic descendants, extending rather than ending the genealogical network.

node.title: Hesiod; instruction addressed to Perses, with myths inside an argument
Works and Days
node.text: A dispute over livelihood opens a poem about justice, work, seasons and conduct. Myth explains difficult conditions; practical advice responds to them. Its sequence is an argument and working calendar, not a continuous mythic chronology…

node.title: The work’s argument
node.text: A dispute over livelihood opens a poem about justice, work, seasons and conduct. Myth explains difficult conditions; practical advice responds to them. Its sequence is an argument and working calendar, not a continuous mythic chronology following the Theogony.

node.title: Reading sequence 1–4 · Hesiod; instruction addressed to Perses, with myths inside an argument
Reading sequence 1–4
node.text: Two kinds of competition · Why survival requires effort · Five races, not a straight decline · Strength is not the whole law

node.title: Two kinds of competition
node.text:
1–41

The speaker distinguishes destructive conflict from rivalry that encourages productive work. His appeal to Perses turns a family dispute into a question about how people seek resources and how powerful judges distribute them.

node.title: Why survival requires effort
node.text:
42–105

Prometheus’ theft of fire leads to Pandora’s creation and arrival. Opening the jar releases human afflictions while Hope remains within. The story explains hardship through a perspective whose treatment of women requires critical attention.

node.title: Five races, not a straight decline
node.text:
106–201

Gold, silver and bronze are followed by a heroic race before the present iron condition. The heroes interrupt a simple metal-by-metal deterioration. The speaker fears a future collapse of reciprocity and respect.

node.title: Strength is not the whole law
node.text:
202–285

The hawk’s domination of the nightingale introduces an argument addressed to rulers. Justice and violent arrogance lead communities toward different outcomes. Divine oversight makes corrupt judgment a public danger, not merely a private transaction.

node.title: Reading sequence 5–8 · Hesiod; instruction addressed to Perses, with myths inside an argument
Reading sequence 5–8
node.text: Work, neighbors and household choices · Observe the season · Profit meets uncertainty · Conduct and recurring time

node.title: Work, neighbors and household choices
node.text:
286–382

The poem urges sustained labor, measured acquisition and reciprocal dealings. Advice on neighbors, gifts and household management reveals assumptions about status and gender alongside the demand to secure a livelihood without exploiting others.

node.title: Observe the season
node.text:
383–617

Stars, weather, animals and bodily experience guide the farming year. Preparing tools and acting at the right moment matter as much as effort. This is situated ancient agricultural instruction, not a modern universal calendar.

node.title: Profit meets uncertainty
node.text:
618–694

The speaker warns about seasonal dangers at sea and recalls his limited sailing experience. Trade promises gain but exposes the household’s resources to loss; prudent timing and avoiding excessive risk frame the advice.

node.title: Conduct and recurring time
node.text:
695–828

Marriage, social behavior, ritual cautions and auspicious days complete the instruction. The closing calendar returns attention to repeated decisions rather than a final heroic event. Its prescriptions belong to the poem’s historical religious world.

node.text: A short heroic encounter expands around an elaborate shield description. Heracles and Iolaus confront Cycnus and Ares with divine help. Keep the traditional attribution distinct from secure personal authorship: the poem’s place in the Hesiodic…

node.title: The work’s argument
node.text: A short heroic encounter expands around an elaborate shield description. Heracles and Iolaus confront Cycnus and Ares with divine help. Keep the traditional attribution distinct from secure personal authorship: the poem’s place in the Hesiodic collection does not settle that question.

node.title: Reading sequence 1–4 · Hesiodic corpus; transmitted under Hesiod’s name, with disputed authorship
Reading sequence 1–4
node.text: Alcmene and two fathers · A dangerous meeting · A world crowded onto armor · Cycnus falls and Ares is checked

node.title: Alcmene and two fathers
node.text:
1–56

The opening introduces Alcmene, Amphitryon and Zeus, distinguishing Heracles’ divine paternity from Iphicles’ mortal father. Its catalogue-like opening places the coming warrior inside a family account rather than beginning with the shield itself.

node.title: A dangerous meeting
node.text:
57–138

Cycnus seeks to defeat and despoil Heracles and Iolaus, but Apollo supports the hero against him. Heracles addresses his companion and arms himself, establishing the cooperation and divine alignment behind the imminent duel.

node.title: A world crowded onto armor
node.text:
139–320

Fearful personifications, fighting creatures, Perseus, cities, dances and productive activities occupy the shield. The description suspends the approaching combat and makes an object carry a dense visual world whose scenes reward comparison with Achilles’ shield.

node.title: Cycnus falls and Ares is checked
node.text:
321–466

Athena warns Ares, but he enters after Cycnus is killed. Divine assistance allows Heracles to wound the god. Ares’ removal demonstrates that this victory depends on a particular alliance, not unlimited human superiority.

Reading sequence 5–5
node.text: A grave that does not endure

node.title: A grave that does not endure
node.text:
467–480

Cycnus receives burial, yet the river destroys his mound at Apollo’s prompting. The ending connects his fate with interference in offerings traveling to Delphi: remembrance itself becomes part of the divine punishment.

node.title: Reading sequence 1–3 · Hesiodic genealogical poetry; fragment numbers here follow Evelyn-White’s 1914 edition
Reading sequence 1–3
node.text: Regional families · A pedigree can become a story · Transmission is part of the evidence

node.title: Regional families
node.text:
Fragments 1–6

The Deucalion and Hellen material connects regional ancestors through kinship. Such genealogies express relationships claimed within mythic tradition; they should not be recast as verified histories of populations or biological descent.

node.title: A pedigree can become a story
node.text:
Fragments 7, 14, 19A

Bellerophon, Atalanta and Europa show how a genealogical framework can open into encounters, competitions and journeys. The surviving pieces preserve uneven amounts of narrative, so detail must follow the evidence available for each fragment.

node.title: Transmission is part of the evidence
node.text:
Fragments 39, 55–57, 78

Later authors quote the poems for different purposes and sometimes report alternatives. Read both the attributed fragment and its transmitting context. A compiler’s selection cannot be assumed to reproduce the lost poem’s full emphasis.

node.title: Rhea
node.text: Hesiod makes Rhea the mother of the children swallowed by Cronus. Ovid names Ops as the mother, by Saturn, of Juno, Ceres and Vesta when explaining the last goddess’ virginity. The family correspondence is explicit in this literary comparison.

node.title: Ops
node.text:
A shared place in a family does not make every festival or attribute interchangeable.

The cited Ovid passage explains Vesta; it is not a complete account of Ops or of Rhea.

node.title: Gaia
node.text: Gaia generates major cosmic powers in Hesiod’s account. Ovid’s sowing-festival prayer addresses Tellus together with Ceres as partners in producing crops. Comparing these passages brings earth’s generative role into contact with Roman agricultural observance.

node.title: Tellus / Terra
node.text:
The comparison moves between a cosmic genealogy and a ritual calendar.

Ovid distinguishes the two partners’ contributions; Tellus should not disappear into the name Ceres.

node.title: Read across each pair; the contrast matters as much as the shared iconography.
Comparisons 19–21
node.text: Helios / Sol · Selene / Luna · No simple Greek counterpart / Janus

node.title: Helios
node.text: In the Homeric Hymn, Helios tells Demeter who arranged and carried out her daughter’s abduction. Ovid’s Fasti gives Sol the corresponding disclosure during Ceres’ search. The sun’s wide vision supplies evidence that other observers cannot provide.

node.title: Sol
node.text:
These passages support a precise narrative parallel rather than a claim that all solar cults are identical.

Hesiod names Helios separately from Apollo; later combinations must be attributed rather than projected backward.

node.title: Selene
node.text: Hesiod places Selene with Helios and Eos among the children of Hyperion and Theia. Ovid closes his March book by connecting Luna’s rule over months with worship on the Aventine. A cosmic family and a Roman sanctuary offer different points of entry.

node.title: Luna
node.text:
Do not erase Selene by assigning all lunar imagery to Artemis or Diana.

Shared lunar functions do not turn a sanctuary notice into proof of identical genealogies or rituals.

node.title: No simple Greek counterpart
node.text: Ovid questions the two-faced Janus about beginnings, entrances, and the opening or closing of his doors in war and peace. Keeping him without a forced Greek counterpart makes the limits of a correspondence chart visible.

node.title: Janus
node.text:
A comparison system must allow an unmatched figure.

Roman religion contains structures that cannot be reconstructed by translating Olympian names.
